doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: White musicians sitting in uptown without reciprocity
summary: Jimmy Dorsey and Jack Teagarden came to Harlem, and Carter explains there was no animosity as it was the tenor of the times.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You mentioned that many of the white players would come in and sit in, and you were not afforded that same reciprocal opportunity. Did you hear Jimmy Dorsey at all?
Yeah, Jimmy Dorsey, Jack Teagarden. Those two stand out in my mind, those two particularly. There were others that I can’t think of by name at the moment.
Was there a feeling among the black musicians, any animosity because of the barriers, that this could not be a two-way street when these people came?

No, I don’t think so. I think we didn’t even think of it. You know, we were just glad that they wanted to play with us, and, you know, we welcomed them, and probably had the society been a little different, they would have welcomed us, the musicians themselves. Yeah, you know, but that was the tenor of the times.
